cim: Colombia Falls in the Artificial Intelligence Adoption Rankings
cim_eredeti: Colombia Falls in the Artificial Intelligence Adoption Rankings
szoveg_eredeti:
In the IMD World Digital and AI Ranking 2026, which evaluated 70 economies around the world, Colombia ranked 62nd in terms of technological competitiveness and future readiness.

For its evaluation, the 2026 World Digital and AI Ranking used 88 criteria: 51 objective statistics and 37 indicators from the IMD Executive Opinion Survey. The data are grouped into five factors: Governance, Technology and Infrastructure, Efficiency, Workforce Development, and Values.

The study, prepared by the prestigious Swiss institute IMD, indicates that Colombia fell four positions in the global ranking of artificial intelligence readiness.

This situation highlights the significant shortcomings facing the South American country in critical areas such as specialized talent development, digital governance, and the efficiency of its technological infrastructure compared with its international and regional peers.

Colombia’s decline is directly associated with significant drops in four of the five fundamental pillars that make up the assessment.

The analysis revealed a disconnect between digitalization goals and the reality of the workforce. Although talent development was the component that received a relatively better assessment compared with the others, the workforce development pillar ranked as the weakest link in the chain.

According to the report, this weakness was based on the country’s growing difficulty in retaining specialized talent in cutting-edge technologies and the lack of effective programs to prepare current workers to use and take advantage of artificial intelligence.

Brain drain and the educational gap in advanced digital skills are taking a toll on national competitiveness.

Colombia ranked 61st in the efficiency pillar, a position that reflects the difficulties in optimizing processes through the use of technological tools.

The technology and infrastructure component remained in an identical position, 61st, highlighting stagnation in the modernization of the networks and systems needed to support the AI ecosystem.

Colombia occupies an intermediate position in the regional landscape. Although it is not the worst-ranked country, it shows a considerable gap compared with the continent’s leaders.

Among the Latin American countries included in the study, Colombia ranked fifth. With this result, the country managed to surpass economies such as Mexico, Peru, and Venezuela, which bring up the rear in the regional rankings, but remains notably behind the region’s highest-ranked economies.

The regional ranking is led by Puerto Rico (73 points, 44th worldwide), Chile (72.7 points, 45th worldwide), Brazil (66.2 points, 54th worldwide), and Argentina (65 points, 58th worldwide).

According to the IMD assessment, the gap separating Colombia from these countries reflects substantial differences in infrastructure quality, regulatory strength, and, especially, the training of highly skilled human capital.

The countries at the top of the global ranking are far ahead. The United States surpasses Singapore and the Netherlands to take first place in national AI readiness. However, the 2026 ranking reveals that national AI sophistication alone does not predict corporate leadership in this field.

The United States has established itself as the world’s leading economy in artificial intelligence, and US companies dominate the global landscape in this field, according to two new IMD rankings.

The 2026 World Digital and AI Ranking places Singapore and the Netherlands immediately behind the United States in the top three positions. In the IMD 2026 AI Maturity Index, which analyzes the world’s largest publicly traded companies, Nvidia retains first place, ahead of Alphabet, Microsoft, SoftBank Group, and Samsung Electronics.

However, a country’s level of digital and AI readiness is not necessarily an indicator of the maturity of the companies based there: some economies with high levels of digital readiness and good governance produce few corporate AI leaders, while companies based in less developed economies can become some of the world’s most mature AI companies.

A related technical report, The New Geography of AI Power, analyzes both rankings together and reveals a more complex picture.
